    Track 0 · Foundations · Lesson 11

    The mental model of an SLM project

    After this lesson you can describe the end-to-end loop of a fine-tuning project, name what each stage produces, explain why the gold set is your single source of truth, and see how the rest of the Academy maps onto this loop.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~8 min Prerequisites: LLMs vs SLMs Verified: 13 Nov 2026

    You now understand the parts. This lesson assembles them into the process you'll repeat for the rest of the course. Training a model is not a one-shot event; it's a loop you go around several times, and most of the work is not in the training step at all — it's in the data and the evaluation around it.

    The loop

    A fine-tuning project has six stages, and the last one usually sends you back to the start:

    1. Data. Gather and prepare examples of your task: inputs paired with the outputs you want. Clean them, format them, split them. This is where most of your time goes and where most of your quality comes from.
    2. Train. Run supervised fine-tuning (usually with LoRA) on a base model. This is the gradient-descent loop from Lesson 0.2, now over a Transformer.
    3. Evaluate. Measure the trained model against held-out examples it never trained on, using a metric that fits the task. Compare the score with the base model's score on the same rows: measure the base before your first run, because that number is the bar. This tells you whether you actually improved.
    4. Iterate. Look at where it fails, fix the data (add examples for weak cases, remove bad ones, rebalance), and retrain. Repeat until the metric clears your bar.
    5. Ship (export & deploy). Package the model into a servable artifact and stand it up behind an endpoint, with a version you can roll back.
    6. Monitor. Watch real-world inputs for drift — the day the live data stops resembling your training data, quality slips and you loop back to step 1.

    Your north star: the gold set

    The most important artifact in the whole loop is the gold set — a curated batch of examples, with known-correct answers, that the model never trains on. It exists solely to measure quality. Every decision ("is this version better?", "did this data change help?", "is it good enough to ship?") is answered against the gold set. If you train on your evaluation data, your numbers become fiction — the model can memorize the test. Keeping the gold set separate and trustworthy is the discipline that makes all your metrics meaningful.

    There is a second, subtler leak. Even a set you never train on gets overfit by your choices if you consult it on every decision: each "keep this change" picks whatever happened to score well on those particular rows. So split the gold set in two. Iterate against a practice (dev) part as often as you like, and score the final (test) part rarely, to report the result. In BrewSLM the gold set is called the answer key, under Data → Labels, and its rows are marked as the practice answer key or the final answer key.

    Key idea

    Modern model-building is data-centric: you usually improve results far more by fixing data than by fiddling with the model. The loop's center of gravity is "evaluate → understand failures → improve data," not "tweak hyperparameters."

    One loop, worked through

    A support team wants a model that routes tickets to one of 8 queues. One trip around the loop might produce this (illustrative numbers, not a measured run):

    1. Data: 1,060 labelled tickets; deduplication removes 60, leaving 1,000. Split: 800 to train on, 100 practice (dev) rows and 100 final (test) rows for the answer key.
    2. Baseline: the base instruct model, with a good prompt, routes 61 of the 100 practice tickets correctly. That 61% is the bar.
    3. Train: a LoRA run on SmolLM2-135M-Instruct. Output: an adapter checkpoint and a loss curve that falls, then flattens.
    4. Evaluate: 84% on the practice rows, a 23-point lift over the base. The confusion table shows most errors are billing tickets sent to refunds.
    5. Iterate: fix 15 mislabelled rows and add 60 billing-vs-refunds examples; retrain; 88% on practice. Only now score the final rows, once: 86 of 100.
    6. Ship: export a versioned model (say v2) and keep v1 to roll back to.
    7. Monitor: each week a reviewer labels 50 live tickets. When a new product launches and a ninth queue appears, the score drops, and you go back to Data.

    Note the sizes: on 100 rows, one ticket is one percentage point, so a 2-point difference between two runs can be noise. The box above says how to tell.

    What "good" looks like at each stage

    • Good data: representative of real inputs, correctly labelled, deduplicated, balanced across cases, with a clean train/validation/test split and a trustworthy gold set.
    • A good training run: a loss that descends and stabilizes, no divergence, a checkpoint saved — and a model that does better on the gold set than the base did.
    • Good evaluation: a metric that matches the task shape, reported honestly — including where the model still loses.
    • A good deployment: a versioned, reproducible artifact you can roll back, with monitoring that will tell you when reality drifts.

    How the rest of the Academy maps to this loop

    Everything ahead is this loop, at increasing depth:

    • Track 1 — SFT fundamentals: the why and what of each stage — datasets, tokenization, the training loop, LoRA, evaluation — in detail.
    • Track 2 — Hands-on: you run the whole loop by hand in PyTorch and Transformers, with no platform, so nothing is magic.
    • Track 3 — With BrewSLM: the same loop, with the platform automating the tedious parts (import, gates, eval packs, deployment) so you can iterate faster.
    • Track 4 — Advanced: advanced moves that bend the quality/cost curve — distillation, warm starts, hyperparameter bake-offs, and proving your SLM is good enough versus a frontier model.

    You can now talk about what a model is, how it learns, how language models produce text, the levers for steering them, and the shape of a real project. Two practical lessons finish Track 0: base vs instruct models, then how to pick a base model. Then Track 1 makes Supervised Fine-Tuning precise — starting with what SFT actually is, and when not to use it.

    Recap

    • A project is a loop of six stages (data, train, evaluate, iterate, ship, monitor), and most of the work is in data and evaluation, not training.
    • Measure the base model first; every run is judged by its lift over that baseline on held-out rows.
    • Never train on the gold set, iterate on its practice (dev) part, and score the final (test) part rarely.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    A teammate tried 12 data changes. After each one they scored the model on the 100-row final answer key and kept the change if the score went up. The final score is now 91%, up from 84%. (1) What went wrong? (2) How many rows does one point represent here? (3) What should they report, and what should they do next time?

    Show answer

    (1) The final set was used as a practice set: 12 keep-or-drop decisions were made on it, so some of the 7-point gain is the changes fitting those particular 100 rows (adaptive overfitting). (2) One row is one point, so several of the kept "improvements" may be one or two tickets flipping by chance. (3) Report 91% as a practice score, not a final result. Get fresh final rows (or set aside a new final split) and score them once. Next time, make all 12 decisions on the practice rows.

    Key terms

    Project lifecycle
    The loop: data → train → evaluate → iterate → ship (export/deploy) → monitor.
    Baseline
    The base model's score on the same held-out rows; the bar a fine-tune must beat.
    Gold set
    Curated, known-correct examples the model never trains on; the source of truth for quality. Split into a practice (dev) part you iterate on and a final (test) part you score rarely.
    Train/validation/test split
    Partitioning data so you train on one part and measure on data the model hasn't seen.
    Data-centric iteration
    Improving results primarily by fixing data, guided by failure analysis.
    Deployment
    Packaging and serving the model as a versioned, rollback-able artifact.
    Drift
    When live inputs stop resembling training data, degrading quality over time.
